divergence: What if the Bering land bridge never flooded?

branches.title: Reindeer Herders Cross Continents
branches.summary: Permanent land allows Siberian reindeer herding, sled design, and cold-climate clothing techniques to spread gradually into Alaska by foot and caravan. Northern communities on both sides develop a shared seasonal round, exchanging breeding animals and knowledge each year.
branches.scene: Herders in fur parkas guide hundreds of reindeer across a wind-packed plain where the sea never formed.
branches.reviewNote: Livestock and sled technology require land; gradual cultural exchange follows directly.

branches.title: An Arctic Ocean Sealed South
branches.summary: Because the Pacific never breaches Beringia, warm currents cannot flow north through a strait and the Arctic Ocean stays colder and fresher. Eighteenth-century naturalists mapping the region document a broad inhabited isthmus instead of open water, forcing new theories of ocean circulation and climate.
branches.scene: Surveyors plant measuring chains across a frozen river valley while Pacific and Arctic waters lap at opposite ends of the same land.
branches.reviewNote: Closed strait correctly alters Arctic inflow and exploration, though climatic effect overstated.

branches.title: Mammoth Steppe Without End
branches.summary: With Beringia remaining dry grassland, mammoths, bison, and horses migrate freely between Siberia and Yukon each season without a sea barrier. Their continuous grazing maintains a vast mammoth steppe that resists forest encroachment long after it vanished elsewhere.
branches.scene: A herd of woolly mammoths crosses frosted tundra below a low sun, breath clouding above calves walking between adults.
branches.reviewNote: Continuous grazing-steppe feedback plausible, but human hunting and warming still threaten mammoths.
